docs.title: 5.1 Loops (general)
docs.text:
Every program you have written so far runs each line exactly once, top to bottom, and stops. Loops are what let a program repeat itself without you copy-pasting the same lines fifty times.

loop: A program construct that repeatedly executes a block of statements, called the loop body, for as long as some condition is true. Each pass through the body is called an iteration.

Think of closing out a register at the end of a shift. You do not write one line of code per transaction in the drawer — you check "is there another receipt," process it, and check again. That check-then-process-then-check-again rhythm is a loop.

docs.title: Why a loop instead of just more code
docs.text:
Say you are handed a stream of numbers — sales totals, sensor readings, whatever — and told to keep a running sum until you see a value that signals "stop." You do not know in advance how many numbers are coming, so you cannot write one sum = sum + val line per value. You need the same lines to run again and again.

🦖 Example

Here is the idea in plain English, before we touch real Python syntax (that starts in the next section). 

sum = 0
val = get the next number

while val is not the stop signal:
    sum = sum + val
    val = get the next number

print(sum)

Every trip through the indented lines is one iteration. The loop keeps going until the condition — "val is not the stop signal" — comes back false.

docs.title: The value everyone forgets to update
docs.text:
The biggest gotcha, before you have even written your first real loop, is this: something inside the loop body has to change on each pass, or the condition never flips and the loop runs forever. In the example above, that something is val — a fresh value gets pulled in every iteration.

Nothing changes, nothing stops

If you write a loop where the condition depends on a variable, and no line inside the loop touches that variable, you have written a loop that never ends. We will hit this for real once we cover if-else branches working alongside loops — the condition logic is identical, it is just checked over and over instead of once.

docs.title: A second flavor: counting values as you go
docs.text:
Loops are also how you tally things — count how many negative numbers showed up, find the biggest value in a list, and so on. The pattern is always the same: initialize a variable before the loop, update it inside the loop, and read the final answer after the loop ends. 

count = 0
val = get the next number

while val is not 0:
    if val < 0:
        count = count + 1
    val = get the next number

print(count)

That "initialize, update, read after" shape shows up constantly once we move into real Python syntax.

docs.title: 5.10 Break and continue
docs.text: Sometimes the cleanest way to write a loop is to give yourself an escape hatch, instead of stuffing every possible exit condition into the loop's own expression.

docs.title: break
docs.text:
break statement: Immediately exits the loop it is inside — no more iterations, no matter what the loop's condition says.

🦖 Example

Searching a nested loop for the first combination of tacos and empanadas that spends a customer's money exactly, with nothing left over. 

max_tacos = 5
max_empanadas = 6
user_money = 20

for num_tacos in range(max_tacos + 1):
    for num_empanadas in range(max_empanadas + 1):
        meal_cost = (num_empanadas * 3) + (num_tacos * 4)
        if meal_cost == user_money:
            break
    if meal_cost == user_money:
        break

print(f'{num_tacos} tacos, {num_empanadas} empanadas')

Output: 2 tacos, 4 empanadas

Notice there are two break statements — one to escape the inner loop, and a second, separate one to escape the outer loop right after. break only ever exits the loop directly wrapping it.

Note

Without break, this same search would need an extra flag variable and a much uglier condition on both while loops. break is not required, but it usually reads cleaner.

docs.title: continue
docs.text:
continue statement: Immediately jumps back up to the loop's condition check, skipping whatever is left of the current iteration's body. 

for num in range(20):
    if num % 3 != 0:
        continue
    print(num)

Output: 0 3 6 9 12 15 18

Every number that fails the "divisible by 3" check gets continued right past — the print(num) line never runs for those values.

How is continue different from just wrapping the rest of the body in an if?

Functionally, not much — you could rewrite the loop above with an if branch wrapping everything instead of a continue. The difference is readability once there is more than one line left to skip. continue reads as "nope, next one" and gets out of the way; a deeply nested if starts eating your indentation.

Easy to miss on a read-through

Because break and continue change control flow without any obvious visual marker, a teammate skimming your code can walk right past one. Use them when the intent is genuinely clearer than the alternative — not just because they are shorter to type.

docs.title: 5.11 Loop else
docs.text:
This one surprises almost everybody the first time they see it — loops can have an else clause too, and it has nothing to do with an if branch failing.

loop else: A block attached to a while or for loop that runs only if the loop finished all its iterations normally — meaning nobody hit a break statement along the way. 

for name in iterable:
    # runs once per item
else:
    # runs only if the loop finished without a break

# runs after everything, break or not
🦖 Example 
names = ['Janice', 'Clarice', 'Martin', 'Veronica', 'Jason']
num_to_print = 2

for i in range(len(names)):
    if i == num_to_print:
        break
    print(names[i], end=' ')
else:
    print('All names printed.')

Output: Janice Clarice

break fires when i hits 2, so the else never runs — "all names printed" would be a lie in this case. Bump num_to_print to something bigger than the list, and the loop runs to completion, break never fires, and the else message prints.

Why not just put that message after the loop instead of in an else?

Because "after the loop" runs every time, break or no break. The whole point of loop else is that it only fires on the clean, un-interrupted finish. It is exactly the tool you want for "search finished and I never found a match" style logic — searching a list for a name, hitting break the moment you find it, and only printing "not found" in the else if the whole list got searched without a hit.

Reserved Words

Treat loop else as answering the question "did this loop get interrupted by a break?" — not "did the condition ever come back False?" Those sound similar but they are not the same thing, and mixing them up is the most common misread of this construct.

docs.title: 5.12 Getting both index and value when looping: enumerate()
docs.text: A for loop hands you the value of each item, but not its position. Plenty of tasks need both — printing a numbered list, flagging "item #3 was the problem."

docs.title: The clunky way, two versions
docs.text:
origins = [4, 8, 10]

for index in range(len(origins)):
    value = origins[index]
    print(f'Element {index}: {value}')

That gets you both, but only by looking the value up manually through the index. Flip it around and you have the opposite problem — the value is right there, but now you need .index() to find its position, which gets unreliable fast if a value repeats. 

for value in origins:
    index = origins.index(value)
    print(f'Element {index}: {value}')

docs.title: enumerate() gets you both at once
docs.text:
enumerate()

enumerate() wraps a container and yields an (index, value) pair on every iteration, so a for loop can grab both without any manual bookkeeping.

🦖 Example 
origins = [4, 8, 10]

for index, value in enumerate(origins):
    print(f'Element {index}: {value}')

Output: 

Element 0: 4
Element 1: 8
Element 2: 10

Cleaner than either version above, and it holds up even if the list has duplicate values — the index is never in doubt.

docs.title: Unpacking is what makes this work
docs.text:
unpacking: Assigning multiple variables from a single sequence in one line — index, value on the left lines up with the two-item (index, value) pair enumerate() hands back each time. 

point = (7, 3)
x, y = point

print(x)
print(y)

Output: 

7
3

This is the same mechanism used any time you unpack a tuple into named variables — enumerate() is just producing a fresh tuple for you on every single iteration.

Do I have to name the variables index and value?

No — name them whatever fits the loop, position, beverage or row, price, same as any other variable. What matters is the order: the position always comes first out of enumerate(), the item second.

docs.title: 5.13 Additional practice: Dice statistics
docs.text:
A capstone-flavored practice problem for the chapter — nothing new to learn here, just every loop tool from this chapter working together on one program.

The task: roll two dice a bunch of times, and print a text histogram of how often each possible sum (2 through 12) came up. This is basically the random number material from chapter 2 wearing a loop-heavy outfit.

docs.title: Building it incrementally
docs.text:
Following developing programs incrementally, do not try to write the whole thing at once.

Step 1 — get the counting logic right for one roll. 

import random

die1 = random.randint(1, 6)
die2 = random.randint(1, 6)
roll_sum = die1 + die2

print(roll_sum)

Step 2 — repeat that a fixed number of times and tally results into a dictionary keyed by sum. 

counts = {}
for total in range(2, 13):
    counts[total] = 0

for roll in range(1000):
    die1 = random.randint(1, 6)
    die2 = random.randint(1, 6)
    roll_sum = die1 + die2
    counts[roll_sum] += 1

Step 3 — let the user keep asking for more rolls, stopping when they enter a number less than 1. 

num_rolls = int(input('How many rolls? (enter 0 to stop) '))

while num_rolls >= 1:
    for roll in range(num_rolls):
        die1 = random.randint(1, 6)
        die2 = random.randint(1, 6)
        counts[die1 + die2] += 1
    num_rolls = int(input('How many more rolls? (enter 0 to stop) '))

Step 4 — print the histogram, using enumerate-style bookkeeping on the dictionary. 

print('Dice roll histogram:\n')
for total, count in counts.items():
    print(f'{total}s: {"*" * count}')

Output (shape, exact counts will vary): 

Dice roll histogram:

2s: **
3s: ****
4s: ***
5s: ********
6s: *************
7s: *****************
8s: *************
9s: *********
10s: **********
11s: *****
12s: **

To Summarize

This one program leans on a nested structure (a for loop rolling dice, sitting inside a while loop that asks "roll again?"), a dictionary for counting instead of a dozen separate variables, and string multiplication to draw the bars. Every piece of it is straight out of this chapter — nothing here needed a new concept, just the old ones combined.

docs.title: 5.2 While loops
docs.text:
Now we write the real thing. A while loop is Python's version of the "keep going while this is true" idea from loops in general.

while loop: Runs a block of code repeatedly as long as the loop's condition evaluates to True. Once the condition is False, the loop ends and execution moves on. 

while expression:
    # loop body, runs while expression is True

# runs once expression is False
🦖 Example 
value = 1

while value < 6:
    print(value)
    value = value * 2

print('Done')

Output: 

1
2
4
Done

Notice value gets checked, doubled, checked again. The moment value is 8, 8 < 6 is False, and the loop is done — 8 never gets printed.

docs.title: Sentinel values
docs.text:
sentinel value: A value that exists purely to signal "stop the loop" — it is not real data, it is a flag.

🦖 Example

A login prompt that keeps asking until the right password shows up is a classic sentinel setup, just checking equality instead of a stop number. 

password = 'star'
user_input = input('Enter the password: ')

while user_input != password:
    print('Wrong password. Try again.')
    user_input = input('Enter the password: ')

print('Access granted.')

The sentinel here is 'star' — the loop runs exactly as long as the user has not typed it.

docs.title: Infinite loops
docs.text:
infinite loop: A loop whose condition never becomes False, so it never stops.

The classic forgotten-update bug

score = 1

while score > 0:
    score = score * 2
    print(score)

score only ever gets bigger. score > 0 is never going to flip to False. This is the same mistake we flagged when loops were first introduced — something inside the loop has to move the needle toward the condition becoming False.

Not every infinite loop is a bug, though. A while True: guard that checks for user input every frame in a game is doing exactly what it is supposed to. It is intentional infinite loops that are fine — accidental ones are the problem.

Reserved Words

Good practice is to write your condition with a strict inequality (<, >) rather than relying on hitting an exact value with ==. An off-by-one increment can sail right past an exact target and leave you stuck forever, but it can never sail past "greater than."

docs.title: 5.3 More while loop examples
docs.text: A few more patterns worth seeing before we move on to for loops.

docs.title: Peeling off digits
docs.text:
% and // together let you pull a number apart one digit at a time, starting from the right. If you have not looked at division and modulo in a while, this is a good moment to refresh it.

🦖 Example 
num = 902

while num > 0:
    print(num % 10)
    num = num // 10

Output: 

2
0
9

902 % 10 is 2, the rightmost digit. 902 // 10 is 90, the number with that digit chopped off. Repeat until nothing is left.

docs.title: Greatest common divisor
docs.text:
Euclid's algorithm is a nice while loop workout: keep subtracting the smaller number from the larger one until both are equal, and that equal value is the GCD. 

num_a = 15
num_b = 10

while num_a != num_b:
    if num_a > num_b:
        num_a = num_a - num_b
    else:
        num_b = num_b - num_a

print(num_a)

Output: 5

docs.title: Random conversation
docs.text:
The random module can drive a while loop too — the loop keeps talking until the user types a stop word, and which branch runs each time is decided by a random number. 

import random

user_text = ''

while user_text != 'goodbye':
    user_text = input('Say something: ')
    reply = random.randint(0, 2)

    if reply == 0:
        print('Interesting.')
    elif reply == 1:
        print('Tell me more.')
    else:
        print('Got it.')
How is this different from the docstring in the raw zyBooks example?

A docstring is just a multi-line string literal, delimited by triple quotes, sitting at the top of a function or program to describe what it does. It does not change how the loop runs at all — Python just skips over it as a statement that evaluates to a string and throws the value away. It is documentation, not logic.

docs.title: Ending on a sentinel that is not a keyword
docs.text:
Same shape as the password example from while loops, but with numbers: keep summing input values until 0 shows up, then report the average of everything before it. 

values_sum = 0
num_values = 0
val = int(input('Enter a value, or 0 to stop: '))

while val != 0:
    values_sum = values_sum + val
    num_values = num_values + 1
    val = int(input('Enter a value, or 0 to stop: '))

print(values_sum / num_values)

Note

That last line will crash with a ZeroDivisionError if the very first input is 0 — num_values is still 0 at that point. Sentinel-driven loops that compute an average almost always need a guard for "nothing was ever entered."

docs.title: 5.4 Counting
docs.text:
Counting iterations is such a common job for a loop that it gets its own section. The pattern: a variable starts at some value, gets updated by the same amount every pass through a while loop, and the loop stops once it crosses a limit.

🦖 Example 
loop_variable = 1

while loop_variable <= 5:
    print(loop_variable)
    loop_variable = loop_variable + 1

Output: 

1
2
3
4
5

loop_variable starts at 1 and climbs by 1 each time. The instant it hits 6, 6 <= 5 is False and the loop is done. That is why the count stops at 5, not 6 — the check happens before the print.

The forgotten update, again

Leave off loop_variable = loop_variable + 1 and you get the same infinite loop bug from a couple pages back, just wearing a counting costume this time. It is the single most common bug in this chapter.

docs.title: Counting down, and counting by other amounts
docs.text:
Nothing says you have to count by 1s upward. Decrement instead of increment, or step by any amount you like. 

variation = 10

while variation >= 0:
    print(variation)
    variation -= 5

Output: 

10
5
0

docs.title: Compound operators
docs.text:
+=, -=, *=, /= are shorthand for "take the variable, do the operation, and reassign it."

Operator Meaning x += 5 x = x + 5 x -= 5 x = x - 5 x *= 5 x = x * 5 x /= 5 x = x / 5

Change the operator and you usually also need to change how the variable was initialized and what the condition checks — a loop that multiplies to count 1, 10, 100 needs *=, not +=, and the condition needs an upper bound that a multiplication will actually reach.

docs.title: Counting shows up in real formulas
docs.text:
A running factorial, a Fibonacci sequence, a savings balance that compounds interest year over year — all of these are just a counting loop with one extra line of math tucked inside the body. 

factorial = 4
count = factorial - 1

while count >= 1:
    factorial *= count
    count -= 1

print(f'4! = {factorial}')

Output: 4! = 24

docs.title: 5.5 For loops
docs.text:
Every while loop we have written so far has been counting or watching for a sentinel. A for loop is for a different, extremely common job: walk through every item in a container, one at a time.

for loop: Iterates over each element in a container, assigning a variable to the current element on every pass through the loop body, until every element has been visited. 

for variable in container:
    # runs once per item in container

# runs after every item has been visited
🦖 Example 
for name in ['Kai', 'Sam', 'Alex']:
    print(f'Hi {name}!')

print('Done')

Output: 

Hi Kai!
Hi Sam!
Hi Alex!
Done

No counter, no condition to write yourself — the for loop just knows to stop when the list runs out.

docs.title: Strings and dictionaries work too
docs.text:
A string is a sequence type, so a for loop walks character by character. A dictionary hands you the keys, in insertion order — you look up the value yourself if you need it. 

for char in 'Yes':
    print(char)

channels = {'MTV': 35, 'CNN': 28}

for name in channels:
    print(f'{name} is on channel {channels[name]}')

Output: 

Y
e
s
MTV is on channel 35
CNN is on channel 28

Note

Looping over a dictionary gives you keys, never values. for value in channels: is a misleading variable name — you would still be getting 'MTV' and 'CNN', not 35 and 28.

docs.title: A running total from a for loop
docs.text:
The revenue-tracking version of what we did with while loops — walk the list, keep a running sum, divide by the count at the end. 

daily_revenues = [2350.25, 1800.50, 1795.00, 2050.25]

total = 0
for day in daily_revenues:
    total += day

average = total / len(daily_revenues)
print(f'Average: ${average:.2f}')

Output: Average: $1998.75

docs.title: Looping backward
docs.text:
reversed() flips the order the for loop walks through, without touching the original container. 

names = ['Biffle', 'Bowyer', 'Busch']

for name in reversed(names):
    print(name, end=' ')

Output: Busch Bowyer Biffle

docs.title: 5.6 Counting using the range() function
docs.text:
For loops walk a container. But what if there is no container yet — you just want to run something exactly 10 times? That is what range() is for.

range()

range() generates a sequence of integers, starting at a value that is included, ending before a value that is not included, stepping by an amount you choose. It takes up to three arguments.

Call Sequence generated range(5) 0 1 2 3 4 range(3, 7) 3 4 5 6 range(0, 10, 2) 0 2 4 6 8 range(5, 0, -1) 5 4 3 2 1 🦖 Example 
for i in range(5):
    print(i)

Output: 

0
1
2
3
4

One argument means "start at 0, stop before this number." That single-argument form is by far the most common one you will type.

docs.title: The negative-step trick
docs.text:
Give range() a negative step and it counts down instead of up — but the start and stop have to flip their relationship too. 

for i in range(10, 0, -2):
    print(i, end=' ')

Output: 10 8 6 4 2

range(X, Y) is never inclusive of Y

range(0, 5) stops before 5 — you get 0 1 2 3 4, never 5. This trips people coming from spreadsheet-style thinking, where a range A1:A5 includes both ends. Python ranges only include the start.

docs.title: What kind of thing is a range?
docs.text:
range() produces its own type, not a list — it is a sequence type like a list or tuple, immutable, and almost always used right inside a for loop rather than stored and inspected on its own. 

sequence = range(0, 100, 25)
print(sequence)
print(list(sequence))

Output: 

range(0, 100, 25)
[0, 25, 50, 75]

That second line is the only reason to ever wrap a range() in list() — to actually see the values it would generate.

docs.title: 5.7 While vs. for loops
docs.text:
Short section, important habit. Both while loops and for loops can count. So which do you reach for? 

i = 0
while i < 100:
    # loop body
    i += 1

does exactly the same job as: 

for i in range(100):
    # loop body

and the for loop version is the one you should actually write.

To Summarize

  • Use a for loop when the number of iterations is knowable before the loop starts — counting down from X, printing something N times, walking a list.
  • Use a for loop when you are accessing every element of a container — adding to every item, printing every dictionary key.
  • Use a while loop only when the number of iterations genuinely is not knowable ahead of time — waiting for a particular character to show up, running until two values become equal.
Why does the textbook prefer for loops so strongly?

Because a for loop over range() or a container is guaranteed to finish. There is no update line for you to accidentally forget — the loop's own machinery advances the position for you every iteration. A while loop hands you full control, which also means it hands you full responsibility for remembering to update the variable, and forgetting that is the single most common bug in this whole chapter.

That said, these are guidelines, not laws. Plenty of correct programs use a while loop where a for loop would technically fit, and vice versa. The point is: if you find yourself hand-rolling a counter with += 1 inside a while loop and the number of iterations was known the whole time, that is a strong signal you wanted for i in range(...) instead.

docs.title: 5.8 Nested loops
docs.text:
nested loop: A loop that lives inside the body of another loop. The outer loop and inner loop each keep their own variable and their own condition.

The reason to reach for this: generating every combination of two things. One item from list A paired against every item in list B, then the next item from A against every item in B, and so on.

🦖 Example

Two-letter domain names — every letter paired against every other letter. 

letter1 = 'a'

while letter1 <= 'z':
    letter2 = 'a'
    while letter2 <= 'z':
        print(f'{letter1}{letter2}.com')
        letter2 = chr(ord(letter2) + 1)
    letter1 = chr(ord(letter1) + 1)

Output (partial): 

aa.com
ab.com
...
zz.com

ord() and chr() are how you step through letters like numbers — ord('a') gives you the underlying integer, and chr() converts an integer back into a character. Worth reviewing representing text if that pair feels unfamiliar.

For every single pass of the outer loop, the entire inner loop runs start to finish. That is why 26 outer passes times 26 inner passes gives you all 676 two-letter combinations.

docs.title: How many times does the inner body actually run?
docs.text:
If the outer loop runs 5 times and the inner loop runs 3 times, how many times does the inner body execute?

15 — not 5, not 3, and not 8. Multiply, do not add. The inner loop restarts fully on every single outer iteration. 

for i in range(5):
    for j in range(3):
        print(f'{i},{j}')

That prints 15 lines total, i staying fixed while j runs 0, 1, 2 underneath it each time.

docs.title: Building a grid
docs.text:
Nested for loops are the natural way to print anything shaped like rows and columns — a rectangle of asterisks, seat labels in a theater, a table of numbers. 

num_rows = 2
num_cols = 3

for row in range(num_rows):
    for col in range(num_cols):
        print('*', end=' ')
    print()

Output: 

* * *
* * *

The outer loop picks the row, the inner loop fills that entire row before the outer loop moves on to the next one.

docs.title: 5.9 Developing programs incrementally
docs.text:
Do not write an entire program in one sitting and then run it for the first time hoping it works. If it has five bugs, you now have five bugs to find at once, tangled up in each other.

incremental programming: Building a program by starting with a small, working version, then growing it piece by piece — testing after every addition instead of only at the very end.

docs.title: A phone-number decoder, one version at a time
docs.text:
Say you are decoding an old-school phone number that mixes letters and digits, like 1-555-HOLIDAY. Do not write the whole letter-to-number mapping in one pass.

Version 1 — just prove the loop actually visits every character. 

user_input = input('Enter phone number: ')

index = 0
for character in user_input:
    print(f'Element {index} is: {character}')
    index += 1

Version 2 — echo digits, mark everything else with a placeholder, and leave yourself a note about what is left. 

phone_number = ''

for character in user_input:
    if '0' <= character <= '9':
        phone_number += character
    else:
        # FIXME: handle letters and the hyphen
        phone_number += '?'

print(f'Numbers only: {phone_number}')

Version 3 — fill in one elif branch at a time, and only expand once the current version actually runs correctly. 

for character in user_input:
    if ('0' <= character <= '9') or (character == '-'):
        phone_number += character
    elif ('a' <= character <= 'c') or ('A' <= character <= 'C'):
        phone_number += '2'
        # FIXME: remaining letter ranges
    else:
        phone_number += '?'

FIXME

A # FIXME comment is a flag for yourself — "I know this is incomplete, come back here." Most editors highlight it specially. On a team, people often tack on a name and date: # FIXME(01/22/2026, Moy): finish letter ranges.

Doesn't writing three versions just take longer?

It feels that way in the moment, but it is faster in total. Debugging one broken line inside a 5-line program is quick. Debugging one broken line buried inside 40 lines you have never actually run yet is a different kind of pain — and it is the kind that eats an entire evening. Small working steps beat one big leap of faith.

To Summarize

A finished, working program should have zero FIXMEs left in it. If you find one after you thought you were done, that is the incremental process telling you exactly where to look next.

docs.title: 6.1 User-defined function basics
docs.text:
Up to now, every calculation you needed got typed out fresh, every single time. That gets old fast, and it gets buggy faster — copy the same formula three times and you will eventually copy it wrong once.

function: A named series of statements that you can invoke by name instead of retyping. def is the keyword that creates one.

🦖 Example

Say you calculate a Fahrenheit-to-Celsius conversion in three different places in a script. Wrap it once instead: 

def f2c(f):
    c = (f - 32.0) * (5.0 / 9.0)
    return c

c1 = f2c(f1)
c2 = f2c(f2)
c3 = f2c(f3)

Notice the main program no longer cares how the conversion is done, only that it can call f2c() and get an answer back.

A function has two halves you need to keep straight:

function definition: The def line plus the indented block underneath — this is where you write the behavior.

function call: Using the function's name followed by () — this is where you use the behavior. It jumps execution into the function and back.

Naming

Good practice is lowercase with underscores, like calc_pizza_area or get_name. Same convention you already use for variables.

docs.title: Parameters and arguments
docs.text:
parameter: A named input listed in the function definition, like diameter in def calc_pizza_area(diameter):.

argument: The actual value handed to a parameter at call time, like the 12.0 in calc_pizza_area(12.0).

A parameter behaves like a fresh variable inside the function — bound to whatever object the caller passed in — and it disappears the moment the function returns. 

def compute_square(num_to_square):
    return num_to_square * num_to_square

num_squared = compute_square(7)
print(f'7 squared is {num_squared}')

Output: 7 squared is 49

A function with no parameters still needs the parentheses, both in the definition and the call — def calc_something(): and calc_something(). Multiple parameters are matched to arguments by position, left to right, separated by commas.

docs.title: Return statements
docs.text:
return statement: Sends a single value back out of the function to wherever it was called from.

  • ✅ return c — hands back one object
  • ✅ return (mean, std_dev) — still one object, just a tuple wearing a trench coat
  • ❌ return mean, std_dev, extra_thing, one_more as if that's four separate returns — it's still packed into one tuple, which is fine, but the function is not secretly returning four things

A function can have return appear anywhere, and more than once, in different branches. A function with no return at all — or a bare return with nothing after it — hands back None.

What happens if I never write a return statement?

Nothing crashes. The function just quietly returns None, and if you try to do math with that None later, that's where the crash shows up — often several lines away from the actual mistake.

docs.title: Hierarchical function calls
docs.text: A function's own statements can call other functions. int(input()) is the smallest example you've already been typing all semester — input() runs first, and whatever it evaluates to gets handed straight to int() as an argument.

docs.title: 6.10 Scope of variables and functions
docs.text:
Every variable you've written so far had one implicit question attached: from where in the program can you actually see it? That question is scope, and functions are where it stops being academic.

scope: The region of a program where a name is visible and usable.

local variable: Created inside a function. Its scope is limited to that function — the moment the function returns, the variable is gone.

global variable: Created outside of any function. Visible from the point it's assigned all the way to the end of the file, including inside functions. 

centimeters_per_inch = 2.54   # global

def height_us_to_cm(feet, inches):
    total_inches = (feet * 12) + inches   # local
    return total_inches * centimeters_per_inch

centimeters_per_inch is readable inside the function with no extra syntax. total_inches, on the other hand, doesn't exist at all once you're back outside the function.

docs.title: Modifying a global variable from inside a function
docs.text:
Reading a global is free. Assigning to one from inside a function needs an explicit heads-up, or Python just creates a brand-new local variable with the same name instead. 

employee_name = 'N/A'

def get_name():
    global employee_name
    employee_name = input('Enter employee name: ')

get_name()
print(f'Employee name: {employee_name}')

Delete the global employee_name line and this program silently prints N/A no matter what you type — the function updated a local copy of employee_name and threw it away the instant it returned.

Use global sparingly

Good practice is to reserve global variables for constants that don't depend on any function — things like centimeters_per_inch above. A function that reaches out and rewrites global state has a side effect that's easy for a reader (including future you) to miss entirely.

docs.title: Functions have scope too
docs.text:
A function must be defined — its def block evaluated by the interpreter — before it can be called. Calling get_name() on a line above its own def raises NameError: name 'get_name' is not defined, the exact same error you'd get referencing any undefined name.

So functions have to be defined at the very top of the file?

Not at the top — just before the first call to them. Most programs put every def block near the top and all the calling code below, which naturally satisfies this without you having to think about it.

docs.title: 6.11 Namespaces and scope resolution
docs.text:
6.10 told you where a variable is visible. This section is the mechanism underneath that — how Python actually keeps track of it.

namespace: A mapping of names to objects — literally a Python dictionary under the hood, where the keys are the names you typed and the values are the objects they're bound to. 

print(globals())

my_var = 'This is a variable'
print(globals())

Output: 

{}
{'my_var': 'This is a variable'}

globals() shows you the global namespace directly, and locals() does the same for whichever local namespace is currently active. Watching my_var appear the instant it's assigned is the whole trick — a namespace only knows about a name after that name's first assignment.

docs.title: Scope resolution order
docs.text:
When the interpreter hits a name in your code, it checks namespaces in a fixed order:

  1. Local scope — inside the currently running function, if any
  2. Global scope — everything defined outside any function
  3. Built-in scope — int(), str(), list(), range(), and the rest of what Python ships with

If the name isn't found in any of the three, you get NameError. This searching process has a name of its own.

scope resolution: The process of checking local, then global, then built-in namespaces to find where a name is defined.

🦖 Example 
daily_cals = 2300

def roll():
    number = 1
    return number

roll()

daily_cals lives in the global namespace. When roll() runs, Python creates a brand-new local namespace holding number — and that namespace is deleted the moment roll() returns.

What happens if I define a function called list()?

Nothing crashes — your list in the global namespace simply shadows the built-in list() for the rest of the file. Anywhere after that definition, calling list() runs your function, not the built-in. It's legal, and it's also a great way to confuse yourself later, so name things carefully.

docs.title: 6.12 Function arguments
docs.text:
Passing a variable into a function does not create a copy of it — Python passes a reference to the same object. Whether that matters depends entirely on whether the object is mutable.

pass-by-assignment: Python's argument-passing model — calling a function binds the parameter name to the same object the argument refers to, exactly like an ordinary assignment statement would.

docs.title: Immutable arguments — safe
docs.text:
def birthday(age):
    age = age + 1

timmy_age = 7
birthday(timmy_age)
print(f'Timmy is {timmy_age}')

Output: Timmy is 7

age = age + 1 doesn't modify the integer 7 — integers can't be modified — it creates a brand-new integer object and rebinds the local name age to it. timmy_age outside the function never knew any of that happened.

docs.title: Mutable arguments — not safe
docs.text:
Lists, dictionaries, and other mutable objects behave completely differently. Modifying one in place inside a function is visible everywhere else that object is referenced, because there's only ever one object — no copy was ever made. 

def add_item(cart):
    cart.append('tacos')

my_cart = ['chips']
add_item(my_cart)
print(my_cart)

Output: ['chips', 'tacos']

  • ✅ age = age + 1 on an int parameter — rebinds a local name, harmless outside the function
  • ✅ cart.append('tacos') on a list parameter — mutates the shared object, visible everywhere
  • ⚠️ passing a mutable object into a function you didn't write and don't trust — read what it does to that argument before you assume it's safe

Protecting a mutable argument

If you need to hand a list to a function but don't want that function touching your original, pass a copy: my_func(num_list[:]). The slice creates a new list object, so whatever the function does to it stays contained.

Why does this matter for business code specifically?

Think of a function that "cleans" a list of transaction records by removing duplicates in place. If you didn't realize it was mutating your original list, you might reuse that same variable elsewhere in your script expecting the untouched data — and quietly work with the wrong dataset for the rest of the program.

docs.title: 6.13 Keyword arguments and default parameter values
docs.text: A function with seven parameters is asking for trouble the moment somebody calls it and swaps two arguments by accident. Python gives you two tools to make that call safer to write and easier to read.

docs.title: Keyword arguments
docs.text:
keyword argument: An argument passed as name=value at the call site, matching a parameter by its name instead of by its position in the list. 

def print_book(title, author, year):
    print(f'{title} by {author} ({year})')

print_book(year=1954, title='The Fellowship of the Ring', author='Tolkien')

Order stops mattering entirely once you're using keyword arguments — Python matches each one to its parameter by name, not by position.

Keyword arguments must come last

You can mix positional and keyword arguments in one call, but every positional argument has to come before any keyword argument.

  • ✅ split_check(125.00, tip_percentage=0.15, num_people=2)
  • ❌ split_check(tip_percentage=0.15, 125.00, num_people=2) — positional argument snuck in after a keyword one

docs.title: Default parameter values
docs.text:
default parameter value: A value assigned in the function definition itself, used automatically whenever the caller omits that argument. 

def print_date(day, month, year, style=0):
    if style == 0:
        print(f'{month}/{day}/{year}')
    else:
        print(f'{day}/{month}/{year}')

print_date(30, 7, 2012)          # style defaults to 0
print_date(30, 7, 2012, 1)       # style explicitly overridden

If a parameter has no default, omitting its argument is always an error — positionally, only trailing parameters can be skipped this way.

Never use a mutable object as a default value

def append_to_list(value, my_list=[]):
    my_list.append(value)
    return my_list

That [] is created exactly once, when the function is defined — not once per call. Every call that skips my_list shares and mutates the same list, so it keeps growing across unrelated calls.

Fix it with None as a sentinel instead: 

def append_to_list(value, my_list=None):
    if my_list is None:
        my_list = []
    my_list.append(value)
    return my_list

Mixing keyword arguments with default values is where this really pays off — if every parameter has a default, a caller can supply just the ones they care about, in any order: print_date(style=1) works fine on its own.

docs.title: 6.14 Arbitrary argument lists
docs.text:
Sometimes you genuinely don't know ahead of time how many arguments a caller is going to hand you. Python has a syntax for exactly that "however many, whatever they are" situation.

*args: A parameter prefixed with * that collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple. 

def print_sandwich(bread, meat, *args):
    print(f'{meat} on {bread}', end=' ')
    if len(args) > 0:
        print('with', *args)

print_sandwich('sourdough', 'turkey', 'mayo')
print_sandwich('wheat', 'ham', 'mustard', 'tomato', 'lettuce')

Output: 

turkey on sourdough with mayo
ham on wheat with mustard tomato lettuce

bread and meat still get filled the normal way, positionally. Everything else the caller passed just piles up inside args as a tuple, regardless of how many extra arguments there were — zero, one, or ten.

**kwargs: A final parameter prefixed with ** that collects any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary, with the argument names as keys. 

def print_sandwich(meat, bread, **kwargs):
    print(f'{meat} on {bread}')
    for category, extra in kwargs.items():
        print(f' {category}: {extra}')

print_sandwich('ham', 'wheat', sauce='mustard', veggie='lettuce')

Output: 

ham on wheat
 sauce: mustard
 veggie: lettuce

Reserved Words

args and kwargs aren't reserved words — they're just overwhelming convention. What actually matters to Python is the * and ** themselves. *condiments would work identically to *args, if that name fits your function better.

Order matters

*args and **kwargs (in that order, if you use both) must come last in the parameter list, after every named and default parameter. Putting them anywhere else is a syntax error.

✅ def f(arg1, arg2, *args, **kwargs): ❌ def f(*args, arg1, arg2):

docs.title: 6.15 Multiple function outputs
docs.text:
6.1 was firm about this: a return statement hands back exactly one value. So what do you do when a function genuinely has two or three things to report — say, a mean and a standard deviation?

You cheat, in the most sanctioned way possible: you pack everything into one container and return that.

🦖 Example 
def get_grade_stats(scores):
    mean = sum(scores) / len(scores)
    tmp = sum((score - mean) ** 2 for score in scores)
    std_dev = (tmp / len(scores)) ** 0.5
    return mean, std_dev

average, standard_deviation = get_grade_stats([75, 84, 66, 99, 51, 65])
print(f'Average: {average}')
print(f'Std dev: {standard_deviation}')

Output: 

Average: 73.33333333333333
Std dev: 15.260697523012796

return mean, std_dev builds and returns a tuple with no parentheses needed — the comma alone is what tells Python to create one. return (mean, std_dev) means the exact same thing, and return [mean, std_dev] would work too, packed into a list instead.

unpacking: Assigning multiple variables at once from a single sequence, matching each variable to the sequence's elements in order — average, standard_deviation = get_grade_stats(...) unpacks the returned tuple's two elements into two separate names in one line.

  • ✅ return mean, std_dev — one tuple, two values inside it
  • ✅ average, std = get_grade_stats(scores) — unpacked back into two names
  • ❌ thinking return a, b is somehow two separate return statements — it's still one tuple, one return

Note

Nothing stops you from returning three, four, or more values this way — return a, b, c is still just a three-element tuple. The function is still only ever returning one object; that object just happens to hold multiple things.

docs.title: 6.16 Help! Using docstrings to document functions
docs.text:
A function with a self-explanatory name still doesn't tell a reader everything — what does it assume about its arguments, what does it hand back, are there any gotchas? That's what a docstring is for.

docstring: A string literal placed as the very first line inside a function's body, wrapped in triple quotes, describing what the function does. 

def num_seats(airliner_type):
    """Determines number of seats on a plane"""
    # function body...

Good practice for a simple function is to keep the docstring on one line, no blank lines surrounding it. Longer, more involved functions can use a multi-line docstring instead — describing each parameter and any special rules about how to call it. 

def ticket_price(origin, destination, coach=True, first_class=False):
    """Calculates the price of a ticket between two airports.
    Only one of coach or first_class must be True.

    Arguments:
    origin -- code of origin airport
    destination -- code of destination airport

    """
    # function body...

docs.title: help()
docs.text:
help()

Pass any object into help() and Python prints out whatever documentation is attached to it. For a function, that means its docstring — plus the parameter list, so you immediately know how it wants to be called. 

help(ticket_price)

help() isn't limited to functions you write yourself — help(str) prints out every method the string type supports, and help(math) dumps the entire contents of the math module. It works with just about anything, because the language creators wrote docstrings for most of what ships with Python.

Is a docstring the same thing as a # comment?

Not really. A # comment is invisible to everything except a human reading the source file. A docstring is an actual string object attached to the function, which means tools like help() — and IDEs that pop up tooltips — can read it programmatically. Comments explain how; docstrings explain what and get surfaced automatically.

docs.title: 6.17 Engineering examples
docs.text: Two worked examples to close out the chapter — same tools from 6.1-6.16, applied to actual physics formulas instead of pizzas and sandwiches.

docs.title: Gas equation
docs.text:
The ideal gas law, PV = nRT, relates a gas's pressure, volume, temperature, and mole count through a constant R. Solve for temperature and it becomes a one-line function. 

gas_constant = 8.3144621  # Joules / (mol*Kelvin)

def convert_to_temp(pressure, volume, mols):
    """Convert pressure, volume, and moles to a temperature"""
    return (pressure * volume) / (mols * gas_constant)

print(f'Temperature = {convert_to_temp(2500, 35.5, 18):.2f} K')

Output: Temperature = 593.01 K

gas_constant is defined once as a global variable outside the function, exactly the kind of use case where a global is genuinely the right call — it's a physical constant, not something any function should ever be modifying.

docs.title: Trajectory of an object on Earth
docs.text:
A projectile's x and y position at time t, given initial velocity v and launch angle a, comes from two standard physics equations: x = v * t * cos(a) and y = v * t * sin(a) - 0.5 * g * t * t. Since the function needs to hand back both coordinates at once, it leans on the same trick from multiple function outputs — pack them into a tuple. 

import math

def trajectory(v, angle_deg, t):
    angle = math.radians(angle_deg)
    x = v * t * math.cos(angle)
    y = (v * t * math.sin(angle)) - (0.5 * 9.81 * t * t)
    return x, y

x_loc, y_loc = trajectory(50, 45, 2)
print(f'x: {x_loc:.2f}, y: {y_loc:.2f}')

A for loop calling trajectory() once per second, checking y_loc > 0 after each call, is exactly how you'd generate the object's full path — and the loop's body stays short precisely because all the math lives inside the function instead of getting rewritten every iteration.

Note

Swapping float() for int() on the inputs here would meaningfully distort the result — angles and velocities in physics formulas routinely need the fractional precision that integers throw away.

docs.title: 6.2 Print functions
docs.text:
Not every function needs to hand a value back. Some just have a job to do — usually printing something — and that's the whole point of them.

void function: A function with no return statement (or a bare return). It still technically returns None, but nobody's using that value.

🦖 Example

Three print statements duplicated across a program get folded into one reusable function: 

def print_summary(oid, items, price):
    print(f'Order {oid}:')
    print(f' Items: {items}')
    print(f' Total: ${price:.2f}')

print_summary(42, 4, 13.99)

Output: 

Order 42:
 Items: 4
 Total: $13.99

The function does its job and control returns right back to the line after the call.

docs.title: Why bother with a print function
docs.text:
The real payoff shows up on the second call. Write the formatted output once, then call it as many times as you need — and if the formatting ever needs to change (adding a !, tweaking a label), you fix it in exactly one place instead of hunting down every copy.

Can a function both print and return a value?

Sure, nothing stops you. Zybooks separates the two ideas here for clarity, but plenty of real functions do both — print a receipt and return the total, for example. Just be intentional about it so a reader isn't surprised.

docs.title: Example: a menu loop calling a print function
docs.text:
def print_menu():
    print("Today's Menu:")
    print(' 1) Gumbo')
    print(' 2) Jambalaya')
    print(' 3) Quit\n')

quit_program = False
while not quit_program:
    print_menu()
    choice = int(input('Enter choice: '))
    if choice == 3:
        quit_program = True

print_menu() gets called once per trip through the while loop, and the main loop stays readable because the menu text isn't cluttering it up every iteration.

docs.title: 6.3 Dynamic typing
docs.text:
You've never once had to tell Python "this parameter is an integer." That freedom is deliberate, and it has a name.

Zybooks

dynamic typing: is used to determine the type of objects as a program executes, in contrast to static typing, which requires the programmer to define the type of every variable and function parameter in a program's source code.

Because of dynamic typing, you can call the exact same function with wildly different argument types and get different, sensible behavior each time. That's polymorphism.

polymorphism: An operation behaves differently depending on the type of the object it's operating on.

🦖 Example 
def add(x, y):
    return x + y

print(add(5, 7))
print(add('Tora', 'Bora'))

Output: 

12
ToraBora

Same function, same +, two completely different behaviors — numeric addition versus string concatenation — because + itself is polymorphic.

Languages like C++ and Java use static typing instead: every variable and parameter's type is nailed down in the source code, and the compiler refuses to build the program if it spots a type-unsafe operation. Python skips that check entirely and waits until the code actually runs.

The tradeoff

Dynamic typing buys flexibility, but it also means type errors don't surface until runtime — sometimes only on the one weird input nobody tested. add(5, "100") runs fine syntactically; it just blows up the moment the interpreter actually tries to add an int and a str.

Python specifically leans on duck typing — if an object can be sliced, indexed, and lowercased like a string does, Python is happy to treat it like a string, no matter what it's officially called. "If it walks, swims, and quacks like a duck…"

docs.title: 6.4 Reasons for defining functions
docs.text: If 6.1 sold you on the "don't repeat yourself" pitch, here's the fuller case for reaching for def even when nothing is actually repeated.

docs.title: Readability
docs.text:
Compare these two versions of the same program. 

def steps_to_feet(num_steps):
    return num_steps * 3

def steps_to_calories(num_steps):
    minutes = num_steps / 70.0
    return minutes * 3.5

steps = int(input('Enter number of steps walked: '))
print(f'Feet: {steps_to_feet(steps)}')
print(f'Calories: {steps_to_calories(steps)}')

versus the same logic flattened into the main program with no functions at all. Both produce identical output, but only one of them tells you, at a glance, what the program is actually doing — the other makes you trace every constant back to figure out its purpose.

Rule of thumb

A general guideline (especially early on) is to keep a function under roughly 30 lines. Not a hard rule — just a sign that if you're blowing way past it, the function is probably doing more than one job.

docs.title: Modular development
docs.text:
modular development: Dividing a program into separate pieces that can be written, tested, and debugged on their own before being wired together into the final program.

This is where function stubs earn their keep — you can sketch out the shape of a whole program's functions before any of them actually work yet, the same way you'd plan a road trip's route before turning the key.

docs.title: Avoiding redundant code
docs.text:
math.sqrt() is the running example of why this matters at all — a square root calculation you never had to write yourself. Every function you define is you handing your future self (or a teammate) the same gift.

Doesn't defining functions everywhere make the program run slower?

Not meaningfully, and that's not the point anyway. Functions exist to make code easier for humans to read, write, and fix — not to squeeze out performance. If speed and readability ever fight each other, readability usually wins until proven otherwise.

docs.title: 6.5 Writing mathematical functions
docs.text:
A function that takes numbers in and hands a number back is the easiest kind to reason about — it behaves exactly like a math class function you'd graph, f(x). 

def height_us_to_cm(feet, inches):
    total_inches = (feet * 12) + inches
    return total_inches * 2.54

docs.title: Function calls inside expressions
docs.text:
A function call evaluates to whatever it returns, which means you can drop it directly into a larger expression the same way you'd drop in a variable. 

def compute_square(num_to_square):
    return num_to_square * num_to_square

c2 = compute_square(7) + compute_square(9)
print(f'7 squared plus 9 squared is {c2}')

Output: 7 squared plus 9 squared is 130

  • ✅ y = 1.0 + square_root(144.0) — the call resolves to a number first, then the addition happens
  • ✅ y = square_root(square_root(16.0)) — nesting works fine, inner call resolves first
  • ❌ square_root(49.0) = z — you can't assign to a function call, only from one
  • ❌ y = print_val(9.0) — assigning a void function's call to y just gives you None

docs.title: Modular math functions
docs.text:
Bigger mathematical functions lean on smaller ones instead of reinventing them. A cylinder's volume and surface area both need the area of its circular base, so write that once and call it twice. 

import math

def calc_circular_base_area(radius):
    return math.pi * radius * radius

def calc_cylinder_volume(radius, height):
    return calc_circular_base_area(radius) * height

This is the same objects idea from Chapter 2 applied at a bigger scale — calc_circular_base_area() doesn't care who's calling it, it just takes a radius and hands back an area, which is exactly why calc_cylinder_volume() can lean on it without knowing anything about pi under the hood.

Fun Fact

math.sqrt() and math.pi from the math module are themselves just functions and constants somebody else already wrote for this exact reason — don't rebuild what's already sitting in the standard library.

docs.title: 6.6 Function stubs
docs.text:
You already met the incremental habit in developing programs incrementally — build a little, test it, build a little more. Function stubs are that same habit applied to functions you know you'll need but haven't written yet.

function stub: A function definition whose body isn't finished — a placeholder that lets you sketch a program's shape before filling in every detail.

🦖 Example 
def steps_to_feet(num_steps):
    return num_steps * 3

def steps_to_calories(num_steps):
    pass

steps = int(input('Enter steps: '))
print(f'Feet: {steps_to_feet(steps)}')
print(f'Calories: {steps_to_calories(steps)}')

Output: Calories: None

pass does nothing except satisfy Python's rule that a function body can't be empty. The program runs top to bottom without crashing, even though steps_to_calories() isn't actually implemented yet.

docs.title: Three ways to stub a function
docs.text:
Approach What it does When to use it pass Silently does nothing, returns None Earliest sketch of a program's structure print() + return -1 Flags itself loudly when called Once other code starts depending on the return value raise NotImplementedError Halts the program entirely When the rest of the program genuinely cannot proceed without this function 
def steps_to_calories(steps):
    print('FIXME: finish steps_to_calories')
    return -1

Reserved Words

pass and raise are both reserved words, same family as def and return — Python treats them specially and you can't repurpose them as variable names.

Why not just skip the stub and write real code from the start?

Because a half-finished real function tends to fail in confusing ways — you can't tell if the bug is in the logic you wrote or the logic you haven't. A stub fails loudly and predictably, and it lets the rest of your program get tested while that one piece is still cooking.

docs.title: 6.7 Functions with branches/loops
docs.text:
Nothing about being inside a function changes the rules you already know — if-else branches and for loops work exactly the same whether they live in the main program or inside a def block. This section is really just proof of that.

🦖 Example — eBay-style fee calculator 
def calc_ebay_fee(sell_price):
    '''Fee is $0.50 to list plus 13% up to $50,
    5% from $50.01-$1000, 2% above $1000.'''
    fee = 0.50
    if sell_price <= 50:
        fee += sell_price * 0.13
    elif sell_price <= 1000:
        fee += (50 * 0.13) + ((sell_price - 50) * 0.05)
    else:
        fee += (50 * 0.13) + (950 * 0.05) + ((sell_price - 1000) * 0.02)
    return fee

print(f'eBay fee: ${calc_ebay_fee(100):.2f}')

Output: eBay fee: $9.50

Same tiered-pricing pattern you'd write with a plain if/elif/else chain — it just happens to live inside a function this time, and the function hands back a single fee at the end instead of printing it directly.

docs.title: Why this combination matters for business logic
docs.text:
Fee schedules, tax brackets, shipping tiers, commission structures — almost every "it depends on which range the number falls into" calculation you'll build for a business ends up looking exactly like calc_ebay_fee(): a branch to pick the right formula, wrapped in a function so the rest of the program can just ask for the answer.

Note

The example above uses a line continuation (\) in the original zyBooks version to split a long else calculation across two lines. You'll rarely need that if you keep each branch's math to one readable line — but it's legal Python if a formula genuinely won't fit.

How many assignment statements run for any single call?

Exactly one — whichever branch matches gets its fee += line executed, and the others are skipped entirely. That's the whole point of elif: only one branch in the chain ever runs.

docs.title: 6.8 Functions are objects
docs.text:
Remember from objects back in Chapter 2 — everything in Python has a type, an identity, and a value. Functions are no exception, which is a genuinely weird thing to sit with the first time you hear it.

function object: def print_face(): doesn't just describe behavior — it creates an actual object, with print_face as a name bound to it, the same way x = 5 binds x to an integer object.

Because a function is just an object, you can do ordinary object things to it — assign it to another name, pass it as an argument, store it in a list.

🦖 Example 
def print_cat():
    print('meow')

func = print_cat
func()

Output: meow

func = print_cat doesn't call the function — no parentheses, so nothing runs. It just creates a second name pointing at the exact same function object. func() and print_cat() are now two different ways to trigger the identical call.

docs.title: Passing a function as an argument
docs.text:
def print_human_head():
    print('o o')

def print_monkey_head():
    print('( o o )')

def print_figure(face):
    face()
    print('| --|-- |')

print_figure(print_monkey_head)

print_figure() never has to know or care which face function it received — it just calls whatever was handed to it. That's the same flexibility dynamic typing gives you everywhere else in Python, applied to functions specifically.

Don't confuse the object with the call

  • ✅ func = print_cat — assigns the function object itself
  • ❌ func = print_cat() — calls it immediately and assigns whatever it returns (here, None)

That missing pair of parentheses is the entire difference between "here's a function to use later" and "run this right now."

Is my_func1 + my_func2 valid?

No — functions only support the call operation (()). They don't support +, -, or comparisons the way numbers and strings do, even though they're objects too.

docs.title: 6.9 Functions: Common errors
docs.text: YES! We all write buggy functions sometimes and its okay. Here are the ones you're most likely to hit.

docs.title: Copy-paste errors
docs.text:
Writing a Fahrenheit-to-Celsius function, then copying it to make a Celsius-to-Fahrenheit function, is a completely reasonable time-saver — right up until you forget to change every single thing that needed changing. 

def fahrenheit_to_celsius(fahrenheit):
    temperature = fahrenheit - 32
    celsius = temperature * (5.0 / 9.0)
    return fahrenheit   # ❌ should be `return celsius`

Everything about this function looks right on a skim — the math is even correct. It just returns the wrong variable at the very last line, because that line got copied from the original function and never updated.

Be extra careful right after a copy-paste

Just like a wet road makes you drive more carefully, treat every copy-pasted function as a small crime scene. Check the parameter names, the variable names, and especially the return line — that's exactly where leftover old names like to hide.

docs.title: Return errors
docs.text:
Two flavors show up constantly:

  • Returning the wrong variable — the function runs with zero errors and sometimes even happens to give the right answer by accident, which makes it harder to catch, not easier.
  • Forgetting to return anything at all — if execution reaches the end of the function without hitting a return, the function quietly hands back None.
def sqr(a):
    t = a * a
    # forgot: return t

Calling sqr(5) here runs perfectly fine and gives you None. No traceback, no red flag — just a silent wrong answer waiting to break something several lines later.

How do I catch a missing return statement before it bites me?

Print the return value the first time you test any new function, even ones that "obviously" work. print(sqr(5)) showing None instead of 25 is an immediate, unmistakable tell — much faster than tracing the bug backward from wherever None eventually crashes your program.
